opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key is to recognize that data like text or images is hierarchically and compositionally structured. Small features combine into larger ones, which combine into even larger ones. In language, letters make words, words make phrases, phrases make sentences, and the meaning at each level depends on how the lower levels are put together. What you'd call an "abstract concept" is something that lives high up in that hierarchy.

When you train a model by predicting the next token, or by denoising pixels, the question is how much data you need before the model can see the correlations that reveal each level of structure. With my collaborators we've studied this with simple generative models of data, which we call random hierarchy models. They're like probabilistic context-free grammars, where each high-level symbol can be rewritten into lower-level ones in several synonymous ways.

What comes out is quite intuitive once you see it. The correlations between tokens that reveal a latent variable, a hidden "concept", get weaker the higher that variable sits in the tree. To detect a weak correlation statistically, you need many samples, roughly enough that the signal beats the sampling noise. So there's a characteristic training-set size for each level. With a small amount of data you only learn local things, like which tokens tend to go together. With more data you can group tokens into "synonyms" because they have the same effect on their context, and that grouping is exactly how you build a representation of the latent variable. Then that representation lets you go up one more level, and so on. The number of data needed grows quickly with the level of abstraction, and the context the model can effectively use grows with the training set too.

This gives one explanation for scaling laws. The loss improves as a power of the data or compute because each time you multiply your data you unlock a deeper level of the hierarchy and longer-range dependencies. It also explains the sense of "emergence": a more abstract capability can appear fairly suddenly once you cross the threshold for that level.

Diffusion models show something similar but you can probe it in a nice way. If you take an image, add noise for a while, and then denoise it, there's a phase-transition-like behavior. With little noise you only change low-level details, like texture. Past a critical noise level you can change the high-level class, so the image becomes a different object, but the low-level features are often reused in a new arrangement. That's a signature of a hierarchical latent structure, and we see it in real images and in text with diffusion language models. Changes are correlated over chunks whose size grows as you approach that transition.

So the difficulty isn't mysterious. Abstract concepts are learnable by local prediction, but only indirectly: you have to infer them from increasingly faint statistical traces, and that costs data. It's a big part of why these models need so much data, and it suggests that architectures or training objectives that exploit the hierarchy more directly could be much more data-efficient.

r001.rationale: It describes learning local token groupings, using them to represent a latent variable, and repeating this process to reach higher levels of the hierarchy.

r002.rationale: It says tokens can be grouped as synonyms because they have the same effect on their context.

r003.rationale: It explains that correlations revealing a latent variable weaken higher in the hierarchy, so more samples are needed to distinguish the signal from sampling noise.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, it's a pleasure to be here.

So the way I think about this comes from a fairly simple picture of what the data looks like. Natural data, whether it's text or images, has a hierarchical and compositional structure. In an image you have edges, edges combine into parts like an eye or a wheel, parts combine into objects, objects into scenes. In language you have characters or tokens, which form words, which form phrases, clauses, sentences, and then higher-level things like the topic of a paragraph or the intent of a document. So abstraction, in this view, really means going up in that hierarchy. An abstract concept is a latent variable that sits high in the tree and that is only expressed in the data through many layers of composition.

Now the question is: what does it take to learn such a variable when all you are doing is predicting the next token, or denoising pixels? And the key difficulty is that the higher the latent variable, the more weakly it is correlated with any individual low-level observable. If I want to know whether there is a dog in the image, no single pixel tells me that. Each pixel is only very weakly informative. The information is there, but it is spread out and encoded in the correlations among many pixels. The same is true in text: the genre or the argument of a text is not visible from one token, it's visible from how tokens are organized together over long ranges.

What we've been doing with my collaborators, people like Francesco Cagnetta, Leonardo Petrini, Umberto Tomasini, Antonio Sclocchi, Alessandro Favero, is to make this precise with simple generative models, hierarchical grammars essentially, where you can actually compute things. The picture that comes out is that learning proceeds level by level. First the model learns low-level features, because those have the strongest correlations with the input, and they can be detected with few examples. Once you have those, you can effectively coarse-grain the data, you represent it in terms of these features, and then the next level up becomes detectable with the data you have, and so on. The crucial point is that each step up in the hierarchy costs you more data. In these models the number of training examples needed to resolve the correlations at a given level grows essentially as a power of the level, so the sample complexity to learn an abstract concept is much larger than for a concrete one. This gives you a mechanism for why these scaling laws look the way they do. The power-law decay of the loss with training set size can be understood as the model progressively climbing the hierarchy, resolving finer and finer, or rather higher and higher, structures as it gets more data.

And this is the sense in which abstraction is hard. It's not that the network cannot represent the concept. It's that with a local objective like next-token prediction, the signal for high-level latent variables is a tiny effect buried in a sea of low-level statistics, and you have to average over enormous amounts of data before that signal rises above the noise.

For diffusion models you can see this very directly. If you take an image, add noise, and denoise it, there's a beautiful phase-transition-like phenomenon. At low noise the model only changes low-level details, the texture, the exact position of an edge. As you increase the noise there is a fairly sharp point where the class of the image can change, the high-level latent flips, while a lot of the low-level composition survives. So the noise level acts like a knob that selects which level of the hierarchy you are perturbing. And the model has to have learned the whole tree for that reconstruction to be consistent. When the model is undertrained, it gets the local pieces right but it composes them incorrectly at higher levels, you get these images that are locally plausible but globally incoherent. That's the signature of a model that has learned the bottom of the hierarchy but not the top.

The same thing happens with language models, I would say. Small models produce fluent local text, grammatical phrases, but lose the thread over long ranges. Larger models, trained on more data, maintain coherence across longer and longer scales. In our framework that is exactly the statement that they've learned the latent variables deeper in the tree.

So to summarize, I'd say the difficulty is fundamentally a statistical one that comes from the geometry of the data. Abstract concepts are high in the compositional hierarchy, their imprint on individual tokens or pixels is weak, and resolving them requires data that grows rapidly with the depth of the concept. That is why you need such huge datasets, and it also tells you, I think, that the natural order of learning is built in: you cannot learn the abstract before the concrete, because the concrete is the basis in which the abstract becomes visible.

r001.rationale: It describes a hierarchy in which low-level features combine into parts and objects, then says the model learns level by level and builds each higher level from previously learned features.

r002.rationale: It does not say that concepts emerge by grouping configurations that predict similar surrounding contexts.

r003.rationale: It explains that high-level concepts are only weakly correlated with individual low-level observables and that their signal is diluted among low-level statistics.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much the concept you want to learn actually helps with the prediction task. Predicting a pixel or a token gives you a learning signal, but that signal need not strongly reward understanding the more abstract structure behind the data.

For example, you can improve many predictions by learning relatively local correlations. An abstract concept might require combining information from many places, and its contribution to the prediction loss might be quite small. So even if the information is present in the data, extracting it can be difficult. There is a distinction between having enough information to learn something and having a learning procedure that can find it efficiently.

Now, that does not mean that token prediction cannot produce abstraction. Clearly, it can produce very rich representations. The question is how the amount of data and computation required grows as the concepts become more complex. Are you learning a structure that lets you generalize to new combinations, or are you accumulating enough correlations to perform well on the examples you typically encounter?

For diffusion models, there is also the question of which noise levels provide a useful signal about large-scale structure versus fine detail. The objective is not equally informative about every level of abstraction. So I would try to understand these difficulties through the strength of the learning signal and the dynamics of learning, rather than assuming that good prediction automatically implies that all the underlying concepts will be learned.

r001.rationale: The response discusses abstract structure and richer representations, but does not say concepts are built by recursively grouping previously learned meanings.

r002.rationale: It does not describe concepts emerging from grouping configurations that predict similar surrounding contexts.

r003.rationale: It explains that abstract concepts may contribute only a small amount to pixel or token prediction loss, making the learning signal weak relative to local correlations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much the prediction task rewards learning the concept. If you want to predict the next word, some predictions require a fairly abstract understanding of what is being discussed. But many predictions can be made using much more local statistical regularities. So you can improve the loss considerably without necessarily discovering the more abstract structure.

And for images, you have a similar issue. There are many details about texture, lighting, and so on that matter for predicting pixels, whereas the underlying concept may correspond to a relatively small part of that prediction error. The difficulty is then to understand when the learning dynamics will pick up that structure, and how much data it takes.

Abstraction itself is not forbidden by these objectives. A good abstract representation can be an extremely efficient way to predict. But the existence of such a representation does not tell you how easily a neural network will learn it. You have to distinguish what information is present in the data from what the learning algorithm can actually extract.

So, from a statistical physics perspective, I would like to study controlled problems where we know the underlying structure and can increase its complexity. Then we can ask whether learning becomes gradually harder, or whether there are thresholds beyond which the model suddenly acquires a useful representation. That would help us understand when prediction leads to abstraction, and when it gets stuck with simpler correlations.

r001.rationale: The response discusses abstract representations and learning dynamics, but does not say models build concepts by recursively grouping previously learned meanings.

r002.rationale: It mentions local statistical regularities, but does not describe concepts emerging from grouping configurations that predict similar surrounding contexts.

r003.rationale: It says concepts may account for only a small part of prediction error, but does not explain that the signal linking increasingly abstract concepts to low-level targets becomes noisier or more diluted, making them harder to learn.
